info.description:
# Introduction

Carbon Arc's [Insights Exchange](https://platform.carbonarc.co/) provides a comprehensive consumption-based platform for accessing decision-making data. Our platform offers extensive collections of insights and analyses that enable organizations to build data-driven frameworks and products while only paying for what they consume.

### Key features
- **Consumption-based pricing**: Pay only for the data you access and use
- **Entity discovery**: Find and analyze brands, companies, locations, and people entities
- **Framework building**: Create custom data products and analytical frameworks
- **Real-time insights**: Access up-to-date insights and analyses
- **Flexible integration**: RESTful APIs designed for seamless application integration

### Resources
- **[Python SDK](https://pypi.org/project/carbonarc/)** - Official Python SDK for Carbon Arc APIs
- **[Tutorials](https://github.com/Carbon-Arc/carbonarc-tutorials)** - Code examples and integration guides
- **[Documentation](https://docs.carbonarc.ai/)** - Complete documentation reference

get.description:
The whole insight corpus in one shot.

Served from the in-process store so the builder fetches once and filters
client-side. Unpaginated on purpose: the previous ``size=1000`` bulk reads
silently truncated a corpus that has since passed 1,200. ``version`` is
also the ETag, so a client holding it revalidates into a 304.

Every insight, but not every field: provider-blocked rows are flagged with
``blocked: true`` per caller rather than dropped -- matching ``/insights``,
which the browse panel renders locked and unselectable -- and the projection
omits ``description``, ``subject_description`` and ``delay_status``.
``/insights`` remains the paginated, searchable listing with full metadata —
it is the public SDK's contract.

Served from the published store; when nothing is published for the current
ontology version the corpus is built live — but only for the response that
actually needs the rows. A conditional request and an already-rendered body
are both settled by the version alone, and a live build made to reach
either was discarded whole.

Everything the builder needs on first paint, in one request.

Unscoped this is the catalog landing. Scoped it is the first paint of a
counterpart browse -- pass `insight_ids` when an Insight selection is
stepping into entities, `entity_id` when an Entity is stepping into
insights -- which collapses that transition's list, count tree and
taxonomy calls into the same single request the landing already uses.

get.description:
Semantically-matched insight ids, in relevance order.

Restores semantic search to the insight pickers (PRO-3373). They had moved
to substring matching over the in-memory catalog, which cost recall — a
query matched "employer" but not "employment" — and silently dropped
everything related-but-not-lexically-similar even on queries that did
match.

Search runs against turbopuffer and returns ids only; the client intersects
against the catalog it already holds, in the order returned. No Neo4j round
trip happens — ``search_insight`` hydrates hits against the graph inside the
vector call, and this path uses a graph-free retriever instead, which is what
moving the corpus into the browser was supposed to buy.

parameters.name: limit

schema.description: Max ranked ids to return. Defaults to full-corpus coverage, which is what a client filtering the whole catalog locally needs. A typeahead rendering a short list should pass its own row cap instead of asking for the corpus on every keystroke.

get.description:
Insight ids linked to the requested entity / event scope.

The browser already holds the whole store from ``/all-insights``,
so scoping a browse only needs graph adjacency: it intersects these ids
with the corpus it has instead of refetching a listing. Adjacency is not
user-specific — provider access is already applied to the store the ids
are intersected with.

Scopes AND together, the same way the paginated listing stacks its entity
and event pre-filters. Adjacency does not vary with subject/topic/dataset
filters, so those are not accepted here — the caller narrows the
intersection it already holds.

``candidate_id`` asks the picker's second question against the same
intersection: which of the entities on screen would empty it. That belongs
here rather than on the entity listing, which is response-cached across all
of its filters — folding a per-selection answer into that key would give
every distinct selection its own copy of every page, for one bit per row.

post.description:
The filter set for a framework.

The job-polling contract is gone from this route for the common case
(PRO-3586): the filter_options precompute artifact answers most
requests, so it runs to completion synchronously under
settings.framework_filters_timeout_seconds and returns 504 if it
exceeds that -- no envelope, no added latency.

PRO-3722: ``poll``/``job_id`` restore the envelope specifically for the
live-fetch fallback that runs on a precompute coverage miss (a real,
occasionally very slow path -- see get_framework_filters' own
docstring). The precompute/cache-hit path is untouched either way.

get.description: Streams a watermarked TXT or PDF built from the canonical text. The response is file bytes, never a presigned URL to the unmarked original.

Live prisms matching a filter, each at its current published snapshot.

Pass ``insight_id``, or ``entity_id`` (optionally with
``entity_representation``), or both to intersect them. At least one is
required: unfiltered, this is every live prism, which is what the
unauthenticated ``GET /v2/public-prisms`` already serves.

**Several results is the normal case**, not an edge. One insight is usually
cut across more than one entity group, and one entity appears in prisms for
several insights. Callers should expect an array of any length including
zero, never exactly one.

Matching runs against what each prism is *configured* to compute, not
against the series it last rendered. The two differ when the warehouse
returned no rows for an entity: that entity is dropped from the chart while
the prism is still, in every meaningful sense, about it.

get.description:
One prism at its current published snapshot.

The same numbers the public prisms page is showing for it right now, out
of the same composition, so the two can never disagree about a prism's
values. They can disagree about whether a prism appears at all, either
way, and only through a stale cache: a first publish whose write failed is
missing from the page but found here, and an unpublish whose delete was
swallowed is still on the page but 404s here. Both lean the safe way -
serve a live prism, hide an unpublished one. Prism ids come from
``GET /v2/public-prisms`` or from the filtered list above.

``data_through``, not the window end, is what says how current the numbers
are: it is the last day of real data in the series and it lags when
upstream sources are behind.

404 covers three states deliberately: no such prism, a draft or archived
one, and a live one that has never published. Only the first is really "not
found", but separating them would confirm that unpublished operator work
exists.

post.description:
Accept a browser tracking event and forward it to Meta CAPI.

Intentionally public: mounted on `public_router` with no auth dependency.
Every caller (`app/power-ui/src/utils/metaPixel.ts`, reached from Cookiebot
consent, the marketing pages, and signup) fires before the user has a
token, so requiring a Bearer would silently break conversion tracking.

Abuse controls, in place of auth:
- `event_name` is checked against `ALLOWED_EVENT_NAMES`
- `@limiter.limit("30/minute")` per client IP
- `TrackingEventRequest` caps every field's length and `custom_data` size
- `email` / `phone` are SHA-256 hashed before leaving this process
- nothing is persisted in power-api; the response echoes no input
- the only outbound sink is `https://graph.facebook.com/v19.0/{pixel_id}/events`,
  built from settings — `event_source_url` reaches the JSON body only

CMP consent is enforced by the caller, not here: `hasMarketingConsent()` in
`app/power-ui/src/utils/marketingConsent.ts` gates `sendCapiEvent`, so a
visitor who declined marketing never reaches this endpoint. A server-side
check is not possible — the Cookiebot decision lives in the browser and any
flag on this unauthenticated request would be client-asserted anyway (PRO-3255).

Ref: PLA-5052 (Shannon audit hash 05faedc8aeb9), reviewed 2026-07. The
public posture is by design; do not "fix" it by adding an auth dependency.

get.description:
The public /prisms page payload. No auth, no per-user data, relative
values only. Proxied from CAMS's serving cache (CAMS owns prism state);
serves the last-good copy if CAMS is briefly unreachable.

Conditional. The page polls this so a recompute reaches a browser that is
already open, and the payload is megabytes of series — so it carries an
ETag over its own content and answers an unchanged poll with a 304.
``no-cache`` rather than a max-age: every request revalidates (nothing is
ever served stale), but an unchanged one costs a round trip and no body.

post.description:
Detach a dataset's catalog role from a principal's per-client role.

The SKU — including its ``catalog`` — comes entirely from the request; the
graph is never consulted. Idempotent: detaching a role that isn't attached
returns ``revoked=False``. The catalog role itself is preserved (other
principals may share it); orphaned roles are the reconciler's job.

Read which principals CURRENTLY hold a dataset's catalog role.

The read-back counterpart to grant/revoke. Polaris is one of the two ways a
client actually reads data (the customer's own query engine talks to it
directly with vended credentials), so a status view that only verifies S3
describes half the access surface.

The SKU comes entirely from the request and the catalog role name is derived
here via the same ``_dataset_catalog_role`` the grant path uses, so callers
never need to know the naming convention, and can't drift from it.

Unlike the S3 bucket policy, where one read covers every client, Polaris
exposes attachment per principal role, so this is one call per principal.
They run SEQUENTIALLY on purpose: PolarisClient lazily caches its OAuth token
in mutable instance state with a check-then-set, so fanning out concurrently
would race on token refresh. Correctness matters more than latency in a
feature whose whole job is to be trustworthy; the cap on principal_names
bounds the cost.

``read_ok=False`` is a 200 with empty lists, not an error, for the same
reason as the bucket-access verify: the caller must render it as "unknown"
rather than falling back to what it intended.

Assign the catalog browse/list roles (``sample_ro_list_role`` and
``bulk_ro_list_role``) to the principal.

Called by CAMS at block-enable. Tolerant per role: if a role isn't seeded in
this environment, logs a warning and reports ``assigned=False`` for it
(HTTP 200). These are list-only roles — they grant catalog browsing, never
data read (which stays per-SKU default-deny).

Grant a principal access to a dataset's S3 bucket by SKU.

Resolves (dataset_id, lag, cut) → dataset_name via
admin_config.bulk_bucket_details and delegates to
BucketPolicyManager.add_principal_for_sku, which is idempotent.

S3-only: ``log_access=False`` keeps PyCAKE off admin_config, so this endpoint
never writes there and read-only PSQL_ADMIN is correct for it (PLA-6141).
CAMS owns the access/audit write, keyed on the ``dataset_name`` returned here.

Compliance gate (runs before any S3 write): the client_name (=clients.key)
must resolve to a clients.id (422 unknown_client otherwise), and the SKU
must not be blocked for that client by the live served-lag restriction
model (403 compliance_blocked otherwise).

404.description: sku_not_found / bucket_not_registered: the SKU has no bucket in admin_config.bulk_bucket_details. Terminal — retrying cannot help.

400.description: Malformed principal ARN, or missing required identifier.

403.description: compliance_blocked: the SKU is restricted for this client.

409.description: policy_apply_failed / policy_write_race: the bucket-policy write did not land. Transient — the caller should retry.

413.description: policy_size_exceeded: the bucket policy hit AWS's 20KB limit.

422.description: unknown_client: client_name is not in admin_config.clients.

post.description:
Revoke a principal's S3 bucket access by SKU.

Either principal_arn (revoke a specific ARN) or client_name (revoke all
ARNs registered for that client+dataset) must be provided. Idempotent —
revoking a principal that isn't currently granted returns revoked=True
with no policy change (mirrors the CLI behavior).

S3-only, like the grant path: ``log_access=False``, and CAMS removes the
admin_config access row and writes the ACCESS_REVOKED audit row (PLA-6141).

404.description: sku_not_found / bucket_not_registered: the SKU has no bucket in admin_config.bulk_bucket_details. Terminal — retrying cannot help.

400.description: Malformed principal ARN, or missing required identifier.

403.description: compliance_blocked: the SKU is restricted for this client.

409.description: policy_apply_failed / policy_write_race: the bucket-policy write did not land. Transient — the caller should retry.

413.description: policy_size_exceeded: the bucket policy hit AWS's 20KB limit.

422.description: unknown_client: client_name is not in admin_config.clients.

post.description:
Read which principals are CURRENTLY on a SKU's bucket policy.

Read-only: never mutates the policy. One SKU maps to one bucket, so a single
call verifies every client on that SKU.

Callers use this to answer "does this client actually have access right now",
which no CAMS-side record can answer — the grant ledger and the sample
settings rows record what we *intended*, and a lost concurrent write makes
the two disagree.

Two outcomes are deliberately 200s with flags rather than HTTP errors,
because the caller must render them as "unknown" and a 4xx/5xx invites a
silent fallback to intent instead:

- ``bucket_found=false`` — the SKU or its bucket is not registered.
- ``read_ok=false``      — the live read failed (throttle, access-denied).
  ``principal_count`` is null and ``present``/``missing`` are empty; do NOT
  read this as "nobody has access".

Defined as sync ``def`` on purpose: BucketPolicyManager is fully blocking
(boto3 + a sync Postgres handle), so FastAPI runs this in its threadpool
rather than stalling the event loop.

get.description:
Entity typeahead over the whole entity store, matched on id and name.

No ``insight_id``: featured entities are pinned independently of any insight.
Served from process memory, with no vector index and no graph on the path --
see ``search_entities_from_store``.

parameters.name: search

schema.description: Entity id or name fragment; empty browses the listing
schema.title: Search

parameters.description: Entity id or name fragment; empty browses the listing

get.description:
The whole insight corpus in one shot, unfiltered.

The picker fetches once and searches in memory instead of round-tripping per
keystroke, so this is unpaginated on purpose. ``version`` is also the ETag: a
caller holding the current one revalidates into a 304 with no body.

Served from the published store; when nothing is published for the current
ontology version the corpus is built live -- but only for the response that
actually needs the rows. A conditional request and an already-rendered body
are both settled by the version alone, which a single node read resolves,
and a live build made to reach either would be discarded whole. Unlike the
entity typeahead a live build here is affordable: it is one bulk corpus read
per version, not a graph query per keystroke.

FrameworkEventRequest.title: FrameworkEventRequest
FrameworkEventRequest.description:
Minimal event primitive for framework compositions.

Wire-layer validator: rejects bad combinations before the request ever
reaches the framework service, so failures surface as a clean 422 instead
of bubbling up as a ``PipelineError`` from inside gateau. The canonical
rule sources live in :mod:`gateau.framework.constants`:

- ``EVENT_REPRESENTATION_TYPES`` — the full set of allowed event reps.
- ``PARENT_EVENT_REPRESENTATION_TYPES`` — the subset valid when an
  ``event_id`` is supplied (since ``event_id`` is the parent event id,
  mapped to fact-table ``parent_event_id``).

FrameworkFiltersBatchItem.description:

``filters`` and ``error`` are mutually exclusive: an item that could not be
answered inside the batch deadline carries a reason instead of a result,
and the caller falls back to the single-framework route for that pair.

InsightLinkedResponse.title: InsightLinkedResponse
InsightLinkedResponse.description:
Insight ids linked to the requested entity / event scope.

Adjacency only — the client already holds the store and intersects
locally, so scoping a browse costs an id list, not a listing.

``incompatible_entities`` answers the picker's other question in the same
round trip: of the candidate entities on screen, which ones share nothing
with the scope, so their cards must be disabled rather than allowed into a
group that has nothing left to query. Only the incompatible pairs are
listed, because on a browse page they are the rare case and absence is the
answer the client acts on by doing nothing.

Absence is deliberately not a positive answer. A candidate the precompute
cannot resolve is omitted for the same reason the adjacency lookup declines
rather than returning an empty list, so a client must read "not listed" as
selectable, never as verified-compatible.

InsightSearchIdsResponse.title: InsightSearchIdsResponse
InsightSearchIdsResponse.description:
Semantically-matched insight ids, **in relevance order**.

Same bargain as :class:`InsightLinkedResponse` — the client holds the
catalog, so a search costs an id list rather than a hydrated listing, and
no graph materialization happens on the search path.

One difference, and it is load-bearing: these ids are ordered by the vector
search's fused ranking, so a client must map over them in order rather than
filter its own corpus by membership. An adjacency filter can keep catalog
order because nothing ranks it; a search result that loses its order looks
broken even when the ids are right.

``truncated`` reports that the search returned as many hits as it was
allowed, so lower-ranked matches were cut.

InsightStoreItem.title: InsightStoreItem
InsightStoreItem.description:
Slim insight row for the whole-corpus store.

Only what the prism and builder pickers render. The per-insight
``description``, ``subject_description``, and the ``delay_status`` dict are
omitted deliberately — they are the bulk of the payload and neither picker
reads them. ``topic_description`` and ``last_updated_timestamp`` are kept
because the browse panel renders the topic summary line and each dataset's
"last updated" stamp.

InsightStoreResponse.title: InsightStoreResponse
InsightStoreResponse.description:
Whole insight corpus, served in one shot for client-side search.

Unpaginated by design — the corpus is ~1.2k rows and the builder filters
it in memory. ``version`` is the graph version stamp and doubles as the
ETag, so a client holding it revalidates into a 304.

InsightsBatchEntity.description: One (entity, representation) the caller wants a listing for.

InsightsBatchItem.title: InsightsBatchItem
InsightsBatchItem.description: One entity's listing, keyed so the caller does not rely on order.

InsightsBatchRequest.title: InsightsBatchRequest
InsightsBatchRequest.description:
Shared listing parameters plus the entities to fan out over.

Mirrors ``get_insights_list``'s query parameters exactly, because that is
the function this delegates to -- one entity at a time, unchanged. Keeping
the names identical is what makes the delegation auditable.

``entities`` is capped because every element runs the whole
``get_insights_list`` path -- Neo4j, Postgres and search -- and the route
fans them out concurrently. Uncapped, one request is a way to hold as many
connections of those shared pools as the caller cares to ask for.

same prism. Extra keys are allowed through on purpose: the body is the stored snapshot entry with display
fields laid over it, and pinning the shape here would silently drop a new
snapshot key from the API until someone edited this class.

position.title: Position
position.description: 1-indexed place in the queue, while queued.

eta_seconds.title: Eta Seconds
eta_seconds.description: Estimated seconds until this job finishes, from recent completion durations. None while no completions have been recorded yet.

queue_wait_ms.title: Queue Wait Ms
queue_wait_ms.description: Time spent queued. Still climbing while queued; frozen at the real wait once the job starts running.

is_heavy_query.title: Is Heavy Query
is_heavy_query.description: PRO-3635: whether the query (or, for a multi-query operation, its heaviest sub-query) scored above the 'typical query' band on pyca's structural cost estimator -- a hint that slowness is query-side, not necessarily system-side load. None if no cost estimate has been recorded for this job yet (e.g. still queued).

poll_after_ms.title: Poll After Ms
poll_after_ms.description: How long the client should wait before polling again. Absent on a terminal state, which needs no further polling.

result_json.title: Result Json
result_json.description: Non-tabular result payload, for jobs whose result doesn't fit QueryJobResult's columns/rows shape (e.g. PRO-3395's batched framework insight queries, each already normalized to plain JSON-safe records). Mutually exclusive with `result` -- a job populates exactly one of the two, based on what its task cached.

max_cell_chars.title: Max Cell Chars
max_cell_chars.description: Per-cell character cap the worker applied to this result's string cells (see truncate_wide_cells), or null when nothing was shortened. Mirrors SQLQueryResponse.max_cell_chars.

truncated.title: Truncated
truncated.description: True if `result`'s rows are a prefix of the real query result -- the worker applied the same byte-payload trim run_query's own sync path uses (see trim_rows_for_payload) before caching, because the result exceeded MAX_PAYLOAD_BYTES. Lives on this envelope rather than QueryJobResult itself: QueryJobResult documents a done job's cached result as always complete, which is no longer true for a trimmed sql_editor job (bugbot finding: 'Async SQL trim hides truncation'), and callers already check SQLQueryResponse.truncated on the sync path -- this mirrors it.

QueryJobResult.title: QueryJobResult
QueryJobResult.description:
A finished job's rows, in the same column/row *structure* as
``SQLQueryResponse`` — columns plus a row matrix — so PRO-3283's SQL editor
migration is a rename rather than a reshape. Note the ``type`` caveat above:
the structure translates, the type vocabulary does not.

No ``applied_limit``/``limit_injected`` here: those describe a caller's
own SQL rewrite, which happens before submission, not anything the job
knows about. ``truncated`` also isn't here -- see
``QueryJobResponse.truncated`` instead: a done job's *cached* result can
now be a worker-applied byte-payload trim (not just a caller's own
rewrite), so that flag belongs on the envelope wrapping this, not on the
row/column structure itself.

QueryJobState.title: QueryJobState
QueryJobState.description:
Job lifecycle, mirroring pyca's ``QueryStatusTracker`` states.

One collapsed ``queued``, with no separate "waiting for a worker" vs
"waiting for the ConcurrencyGate" state (PRO-3278 decision): the two are
indistinguishable to the person waiting.

Be aware of where the worker actually draws that line today. It calls
``mark_running`` *before* ``async_read_query``, and the gate is acquired
inside that call, so a job parked on the gate reports ``running`` — with no
position, no ETA, and a ``queue_wait_ms`` frozen at pickup — rather than
``queued``. Under a saturated gate, which is the condition this whole system
exists to make visible, that understates the wait by exactly the gate wait.
Moving ``mark_running`` past gate admission is a change to the worker
(PRO-3281), tracked separately.

An enum rather than a bare ``str`` so a state pyca adds later surfaces as
a loud, explicit failure in ``QueryJobService`` instead of flowing through
to clients that have no branch for it.
